sections.description: A recap of representing linear transformations with matrices, where a transformation is determined by the images of the basis vectors i-hat and j-hat, and those images form the columns of the matrix. The computation of how any vector transforms reduces to combining those column images proportionally to its coordinates.
sections.title: Recap: Linear transformations and matrix basics

concepts: composition matrix as the overall effect
sections.description: When two linear transformations are applied in sequence, the result is another linear transformation. The video shows a rotation followed by a shear and explains that this overall effect can be captured by a single matrix, whose columns are the final positions of i-hat and j-hat after both transformations.
sections.title: Composition of transformations and the composition matrix

concepts: first column of composition = left matrix times first column of right matrix

concrete example with M1 and M2
evidence that the composition matrix encodes the same net transformation as applying M1 then M2
sections.description: The presenter shows how to obtain the composition matrix by analyzing where i-hat and j-hat land after applying M1 and then M2. The first column is found by multiplying M1 by the first column of M2 (the image of i-hat), and the second column by multiplying M1 by the second column of M2 (the image of j-hat). A concrete M1/M2 example demonstrates this column-by-column construction.
sections.title: Computing the composition matrix from M1 and M2 (column-by-column process)

sections.description: The speaker extends the reasoning to symbolic matrices to illustrate that the same column-based logic applies generally. He emphasizes the geometric interpretation of matrix multiplication as applying one transformation after another, the necessity of reading from right to left, the fact that order matters, and why associativity is natural from this viewpoint. The video ends by foreshadowing extensions beyond two dimensions.
sections.title: Symbolic generalization, intuition, and conclusions

summary: This video explains how linear transformations are represented by matrices, focusing on composing transformations as a single matrix. It reviews that a linear transformation is determined by its action on the basis vectors (i-hat, j-hat) and that a matrix’s columns encode where those basis vectors land after the transformation. The core idea is that composing two linear transformations—such as a rotation followed by a shear—yields a new linear transformation that can itself be described by a matrix, the “composition matrix.” The video demonstrates constructing this matrix by tracking how i-hat and j-hat are mapped through each transformation, shows how matrix multiplication implements the sequential application of transformations (read right-to-left), and provides concrete examples (M1 and M2) to compute the composition matrix column by column. It also discusses why the order matters and how associativity of matrix multiplication arises from thinking about applying transformations, with a symbolic generalization and a teaser for extending the ideas beyond two dimensions.
title: Matrix multiplication as composition (Essence of Linear Algebra, Chapter 4)
